name: Chemical peels for acne

lead: Chemical peels apply acids such as salicylic, glycolic, Jessner solution or TCA to remove the top skin layers. People use them to clear acne, cut oil, and fade acne marks and scars for smoother, clearer skin, in clinics or at lower strengths at home.

The controlled injury sheds the outer layers, unclogging pores and speeding turnover. Salicylic acid is the agent most associated with acne; it is oil-soluble and described as antibacterial and anti-inflammatory. Small clinical studies have compared peels for acne, while a general skincare reference describes the evidence as insufficient to recommend them. Dermatologists sometimes use them alongside medical treatment.

paras: Clinic peels are applied by a dermatologist or trained professional, often as a series, and lower-strength versions are sold for home use. Peeling and redness are expected for a period afterwards.

Reported risks include redness, photosensitivity, pigment changes, milia and scarring, including from low-strength home kits. Concern about pigment complications has limited medium-depth peel use in darker skin.

angle.text: Peels exfoliate the outer skin, unclogging pores and speeding cell turnover so acne clears and texture smooths. Small studies exist for acne, while guidelines describe the evidence as insufficient.

lead: A chemical peel is a treatment, most often applied to the face, in which a chemical agent removes the outer skin layers; the controlled injury causes peeling and can smooth texture and reduce acne scars and pigmentation.[1] For acne, the agents most often discussed are salicylic acid (a beta hydroxy acid), glycolic acid (an alpha hydroxy acid), Jessner solution and trichloroacetic acid (TCA), used in a dermatology office or, at lower strengths, at home.[1]

Salicylic acid is oil-soluble, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory, and is described as increasingly preferred over alpha hydroxy acids for acne.[1] Small clinical studies have compared peels for acne, but a general skincare reference states that evidence is insufficient to recommend chemical peels for acne, although dermatologists sometimes use them alongside medical treatment.[2]
infobox: Peeling introduced by Ferdinand von Hebra, 19th century

paras: Alpha hydroxy acid peels such as glycolic acid are the mildest and are used for fine wrinkles, uneven pigment and acne. Beta hydroxy acid peels use salicylic acid. Medium-depth TCA peels are performed in offices or outpatient centres and can be more uncomfortable. Phenol-croton oil peels are deep peels.[1] Jessner solution is a combination peel often used in dermatology clinics, sometimes as a preparatory step before deeper peels.[1]

In appearance-focused communities peels are discussed as a way to treat active acne, post-acne marks and texture, with some users using professionally applied peels and others using lower-strength products at home. Reports of results vary between users.

Deeper peels carry more risk. Possible complications include photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia, skin thinning and texture changes; both professional peels and low-strength home kits can cause injury and scarring.[1] Researchers describing a TCA technique note that fear of pigmentary complications and scarring has limited use of medium-depth peels in darker skin.[3]

A comparative study of 20 patients aged 13 to 30 with acne vulgaris examined the effect of 50% pyruvic and 30% salicylic acid peels on facial sebum secretion.[4] A technique paper describes a TCA peel approach for light and dark skin, but it is not specific to acne.[3]

Several trials registered with ClinicalTrials.gov compare peels for acne, including 25% TCA versus 30% salicylic acid in mild to moderate acne (60 participants), a trial of different peel types in acne vulgaris (90 participants), a crystal peel in adults with mild acne (42 participants), and combined salicylic and azelaic acid versus 25% TCA (34 participants).[5][6][7][8] Registrations describe study design rather than results. A 2025-registered trial plans to compare glycolic and salicylic peels for post-acne scars.[9] A general skincare overview states that evidence is insufficient to recommend peels for acne.[2]

lore.intro: Peels are discussed in skin-focused looksmaxxing spaces as an in-office or home option for acne and acne marks.[1]

claims.claim: Salicylic acid peels clear acne and control oil.
Home peels give results similar to professional ones.

timeline.event: Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra introduces chemical peeling with agents such as phenol, croton oil and nitric acid.[1]
